source.title: Early-Learning Regularization Prevents Memorization of Noisy Labels
source.authors: Sheng Liu; Jonathan Niles-Weed; Narges Razavian; C. Fernandez-Granda

record.file_problem: Text contains the full paper and supplementary sections; no obvious garbling or cutoff.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports its own results on early learning followed by memorization of noisy labels, and tests a regularizer designed to prevent that memorization. Its evidence refines the claim to a specified noisy-label setting and method.
record.gate_note: The study directly trains networks with randomly corrupted labels and describes their training behavior. Its main benchmark tables report test accuracy, not training error on fully random labels. Results comparing ELR and ELR+ with other methods are not rows unless they report what cross-entropy-trained models themselves do. Cited findings from Arpit et al. and Zhang et al. are not extracted as this study's results.
record.test_reason: The study's own ResNet-34 training trajectories directly test V6 at 40% random label corruption. It also develops a theoretical explanation using linear classification. Its mitigation benchmarks do not establish the fully random-label claims or V4's joint training-fit and test-error trajectory.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is accurate with a scope clarification: the theoretical characterization applies to a specified high-dimensional linear generative model, rather than proving the phenomenon for deep networks generally. The authors use these insights to design ELR and report strong noisy-label benchmark performance; they explicitly leave bridging linear and nonlinear theory open.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies noisy-label training and proposes an additional ELR regularization term with temporal targets; it does not reproduce the original random-label experiments. It evaluates 40% and other corruption levels, not completely random labels.
record.method_sensitivity: Noise fraction; dataset and architecture; training procedure and learning-rate schedule; ELR target averaging and regularization hyperparameters; mixup, weight averaging, and use of two networks.

fits_no_version.finding: Linear softmax regression exhibits early true-class learning followed by noisy-label memorization; the theory proves this sequence under specified Gaussian-mixture and dimensional assumptions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Early learning followed by memorization also occurs in high-dimensional linear classification, under suitable signal and dimensional conditions.

fits_no_version.finding: ELR prevents noisy-label memorization while preserving learning of true classes in the illustrated deep and linear models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A regularizer designed around early predictions can suppress later memorization under partial label corruption.

record.problems: The directly described training trajectories are qualitative and shown in figures, without numerical training-error curves in text. The full-random-label condition and test error at chance are not reported. The benchmark tables focus on test accuracy and do not provide training errors; some cross-method table results are taken from prior papers. The paper notes that results from other methods may not be completely comparable because evaluation protocols differ.
record.rows_left_out: Table 1 contains many method-by-noise benchmark values and Table 2 contains numerous method-by-noise test accuracies. Only the cross-entropy comparator values for 40% symmetric noise and a subset of CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100 noise levels are retained; the table values do not report the training-error behavior named in the versions, and Table 1's flattened layout obscures the two metric columns. Other methods' results are comparative method results rather than outcomes of the claim's object. No separate rows extracted for real-world datasets because they do not vary label corruption rates in the reported results.

untested.parts: Completely random labels, zero or near-zero training error with unchanged architecture and hyperparameters, and chance test performance.
Training time relative to true-label fitting and convergence time as corruption increases. Table I.1 compares methods at fixed noise, not clean versus random labels.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or unstructured Gaussian-noise inputs.
Perfect training fit combined with steadily worsening test error across corruption levels from zero to complete randomization. The extracted cross-entropy benchmark sequences are cited results.
Whether weight decay, dropout, and augmentation prevent random-label fitting, and whether removing these practices harms true-label generalization. ELR is a different, purpose-built regularizer.
Completely random-label training and a direct comparison of wholly random-label and true-label learning trajectories; broader generality beyond the demonstrated deep-network setting.

record.verdict_notes: Only the supplied text was used. Figure images are not available here, so the trajectory verdict relies on their explicit captions and accompanying prose. The absence of full-randomization experiments is untested scope, not contrary evidence.

versions.untested_parts: The paper illustrates a ResNet-34 trained with cross-entropy on CIFAR-10 with 40% randomly flipped labels and states that it eventually memorizes wrong labels, but does not give a separately extractable numerical training error or test error at chance for completely random labels. The fully random-label and unchanged-hyperparameter condition is not tested.

The paper varies corruption rates in benchmark comparisons, but the reported tables give test accuracies across methods, not training-set perfection or a direct steadily rising test-error curve for the same network.
The study uses weight decay and data augmentation in its experiments but does not test whether those practices prevent fitting random labels or whether removing them harms true-label generalization.

Tests noisy labels at 40% corruption in CIFAR-10 and a simulated linear classification task; it does not test completely random labels or compare learning on true labels versus wholly random labels over training.

rows.subject: ResNet-34
rows.operation_detail: Trained with cross-entropy on CIFAR-10 with 40% randomly flipped labels; authors describe early learning followed by memorization.
rows.measure: Training-set prediction fractions for clean-label and wrong-label examples over training, described qualitatively.
rows.value: Begins by predicting true labels, including many wrong-label examples, then eventually memorizes wrong labels.
rows.note: Figure 1 describes the training trajectories; no numerical training-error values are provided in the text.
rows.check: The qualitative trajectory is correctly extracted: predictions initially follow true labels, including on mislabeled examples, before fitting the incorrect supplied labels. Exact training-error values are unavailable.

rows.subject: two-class softmax regression model
rows.operation_detail: Trained with cross-entropy on simulated Gaussian-mixture data with randomly flipped labels.
rows.measure: Training accuracy on clean-label and wrong-label examples over training, described qualitatively.
rows.value: Begins by learning true labels, then eventually memorizes the examples with wrong labels.
rows.locator: Figure A.1 caption; Sections 3 and B
rows.note: Supplementary Figure A.1 describes the trajectory but gives no numerical accuracy values in text.
rows.check: The trajectory is correctly described, but the subject is linear softmax regression, rather than the deep networks named by the versions. A single corruption level also cannot establish V4.

rows.subject: ResNet-34
rows.operation_detail: Trained using early-learning regularization (ELR) on CIFAR-10 with 40% randomly flipped labels.
rows.measure: Training-set prediction fractions for clean-label and wrong-label examples over training, described qualitatively.
rows.baseline: Cross-entropy model begins to memorize wrong labels.
rows.value: Regularization prevents memorization and allows continued learning on examples with clean labels, attaining high accuracy on clean- and wrong-label examples.
rows.note: The outcome is qualitative; the paper does not provide training error values establishing perfect fit across the corrupted training set.
rows.check: This is the proposed mitigation's outcome, not a test of V4's corruption-rate trajectory. High accuracy on wrong-label examples means agreement with their true classes, not successful fitting of their supplied incorrect labels.

rows.subject: two-class softmax regression model
rows.operation_detail: Trained using ELR with temporal ensembling on simulated Gaussian-mixture data.
rows.measure: Training accuracy on clean-label and wrong-label examples over training, described qualitatively.
rows.baseline: Cross-entropy model eventually memorizes wrong labels.
rows.value: ELR prevents memorization and allows continued learning, attaining high accuracy on clean- and wrong-label examples.
rows.note: Qualitative figure description; no numerical accuracy values stated.
rows.check: This is mitigation performance in a linear model, not the deep-network behavior named by V4. Accuracy is evaluated against true classes, including for mislabeled examples.
